        17                  THE SECRETARY:    By Senator

        18       Stewart-Cousins, legislative resolution

        19       honoring Dr. Olivia J. Hooker upon the

        20       occasion of her selection as a New York State

        21       Woman of Distinction, in conjunction with

        22       March as Women's History Month, and marking

        23       March 24, 2010, as "Oliva J. Hooker Day" in

        24       the State of New York.

        25                  ACTING SENATOR VALESKY:    Senator



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1926



         1       Stewart-Cousins, on the resolution.

         2                  SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:    Thank

         3       you, Mr. President.

         4                  It is such an honor to stand here

         5       today and recognize my constituent and,

         6       frankly, a jewel of the entire State of

         7       New York and the country, Dr. Olivia J.

         8       Hooker.

         9                  I have the privilege of saying, as

        10       I said, that Dr. Olivia Hooker is my

        11       constituent.  But Dr. Hooker means so much to

        12       American history and certainly women's

        13       history, I thought it was important to bring

        14       her today to get the accolades she so richly

        15       deserves in the State Capitol.

        16                  I have known Dr. Hooker because

        17       Dr. Hooker is a woman who is never too busy to

        18       be part of whatever is going on, especially if

        19       it's giving of herself.  But it was at a Black

        20       History Month celebration last month that I

        21       got to hear more dimensions of Dr. Olivia J.

        22       Hooker.

        23                  Now, Dr. Hooker is a clinical

        24       psychologist.  Dr. Hooker taught as an

        25       associate professor at Fordham University for



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1927



         1       22 years.  Dr. Hooker was part of state

         2       government when she worked in Bedford

         3       facilities with women with psychological

         4       problems.  Dr. Hooker has been a pioneer in

         5       every phase of her life.

         6                  But the story that she told in

         7       February was about her life as a child in

         8       Tulsa, Oklahoma.  What she told us was about

         9       the Tulsa, Oklahoma, race riots, where 300

        10       were killed and a thousand homes and

        11       businesses owned by blacks in Tulsa, Oklahoma,

        12       were burned to the ground.

        13                  What Dr. Hooker described was what

        14       is known as "Black Wall Street."  And Black

        15       Wall Street, because of the segregation,

        16       actually thrived, because there was nowhere

        17       else for the black community to go and grow.

        18       Dr. Hooker's father was a clothier.  And all

        19       of the professionals were doing so well and

        20       apparently became kind of the envy of

        21       surrounding Tulsa communities.

        22                  And there was a fateful night in

        23       1921, in May, where something happened that

        24       sparked a racial incident.  And the rest, as

        25       Dr. Hooker will tell us, unfortunately isn't



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1928



         1       history.

         2                  Yes, 300 people were killed, more

         3       than any killed in all of the race riots in

         4       our country combined.  And yes, there was the

         5       total decimation of black businesses and

         6       homes.  And Dr. Hooker's family had to move to

         7       Kansas, along with so many other families that

         8       moved other places, because not even the

         9       schools were left intact.  They were bombed.

        10                  But Dr. Hooker's family moved, she

        11       went on.  She received her education and

        12       decided at that point that there was not

        13       enough that she could do to better herself,

        14       work for other people, and serve her country.

        15       Dr. Hooker decided that she wanted to join the

        16       armed forces and became, in 1945, the very

        17       first African-American woman to serve in the

        18       Coast Guard.

        19                  And after she broke that barrier

        20       and went on to teach and instruct and to heal,

        21       Dr. Hooker -- who, again, was born in 1915 --

        22       decided in 1997 that it was time for people to

        23       understand what happened in Tulsa because it

        24       was so much a part of American history.

        25                  She was able, with about 103 others



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1929



         1       who had also been through the Tulsa race

         2       riots, to advance a court proceeding in the

         3       hopes that there would be some restitution or

         4       at least some acknowledgment of what happened

         5       in Tulsa, Oklahoma.  She was able to get

         6       people like Johnny Cochran, the late Johnny

         7       Cochran involved in her case; Dr. John Hope

         8       Franklin, noted historian, certainly advisor

         9       to presidents; Dr. Charles Ogletree, a

        10       wonderful Harvard professor.  Some of the most

        11       brilliant minds came together in order to

        12       advance the case of what happened in Tulsa,

        13       Oklahoma.

        14                  Dr. Hooker testified in front of

        15       Congress.  And Dr. Hooker and others went to

        16       the Supreme Court in the hopes that there

        17       would be some hearing of the case.  The case

        18       was not heard because of the statute of

        19       limitations.  But there was a documentary made

        20       called "Before They Die."

        21                  And Dr. Hooker has dedicated her

        22       life to teaching, telling, demonstrating what

        23       a life well-lived means in all of its aspects.

        24                  Today she spent time with the

        25       interns in the Capitol.  Today she taught



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1930



         1       young people who were beginning lives in

         2       public service how important that service is

         3       and how important it is that when there's an

         4       obstacle, no matter how difficult, that you

         5       just move forward in a positive way and the

         6       doors will open.

         7                  Dr. Hooker told these young people

         8       today, as she'll tell by her presence all of

         9       us, that it doesn't help to hold grudges, it

        10       doesn't help to be angry.  That what any

        11       difficulty means is that you have to seek the

        12       opportunities and, when they come, take them

        13       and be ready.  And even if you think that an

        14       opportunity that you have at a moment is not

        15       really necessary for that moment, you'll be

        16       surprised how helpful it will be when you

        17       really need it.

        18                  Dr. Hooker, at 95, jumped at the

        19       chance to be here today, to meet all of us, to

        20       speak to the interns, to talk about what

        21       happened at Tulsa, to tell us all in the

        22       presence of such a great woman how easy it is

        23       to still be humble while you give so much of

        24       your life.

        25                  So I am so proud of Dr. Hooker, so



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1931



         1       pleased that she is our constituent, all of

         2       us, so pleased that she has so nobly walked

         3       through the country telling a story, but

         4       telling it with love.  Because as Dr. Hooker

         5       says, the only way people really learn, even

         6       if they're being admonished, is with love.

         7                  So again, it is my privilege to

         8       welcome Dr. Hooker here.

         9                  Thank you, Mr. President.

        23       Oppenheimer, legislative resolution honoring

        24       Katherine Kornblum as one of the World War II

        25       WASP female pilots to receive a Congressional



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1933



         1       Gold Medal on March 10, 2010.

         2                  ACTING SENATOR VALESKY:    Senator

         3       Oppenheimer, on the resolution.

         4                  SENATOR OPPENHEIMER:    Thank you

         5       very much.

         6                  I would just like to say before I

         7       speak on this resolution that I've worked with

         8       Dr. Hooker on some very wonderful social

         9       service childcare initiatives, and she is a

        10       dynamo.  And I think she has more energy than

        11       I have.  So I thought I should pay tribute to

        12       Dr. Hooker and tell her she's extraordinary

        13       and keep up her good work.

        14                  But I'd like to talk on someone who

        15       could not come here today.  She's actually

        16       three years younger than Dr. Hooker, but she

        17       didn't feel that she could make the trip up

        18       from Westchester.  And she has quite an

        19       amazing story to tell, which I'll briefly

        20       paraphrase.

        21                  Katherine Kornblum was one of the

        22       World War II WASP female pilots, and she

        23       received the Congressional Gold Medal just

        24       fairly recently -- actually, what am I saying,

        25       two weeks ago, at a ceremony that was held in



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1934



         1       Washington, D.C.

         2                  And there were a couple of

         3       pioneering organizations of civilian female

         4       pilots employed to fly military aircraft under

         5       the direction of the Army Air Force during the

         6       Second World War.  And these female pilots

         7       each already had a pilot's license, but they

         8       were trained to fly the Army way in

         9       Sweetwater, Texas.  And actually over a

        10       thousand of them earned their wings and became

        11       the first women to fly American military

        12       aircraft.

        13                  And the WASPs were stationed at 120

        14       air bases across the United States.  They were

        15       relieving the male pilots who were going into

        16       combat duty, and they were for the most part

        17       doing operational things between American

        18       aircraft factories and military bases in

        19       Europe and other places.  And that freed the

        20       men to go into actual warfare.

        21                  But these pilots were quite

        22       remarkable for their time.  And President

        23       Obama awarded these WASPs -- there are now 38

        24       of them -- these female pilots the

        25       Congressional Gold Medal.  And I think Ruth



                      Candyco Transcription Service, Inc.
                                                         1935



         1       believes that she flew over 1,000 hours for

         2       her country during the Second World War.

         3                  And now, I mean at 92, she's quite

         4       remarkable.  Because for the last over a

         5       decade -- maybe a decade and a half now --

         6       she's been volunteering at Sarah Neuman

         7       Nursing Home in Mamaroneck, a few blocks from

         8       my house, and she works there several days a

         9       week doing clerical work and dealing with the

        10       patients there.

        11                  So a remarkable woman who we are

        12       happy to honor and certainly has an amazing

        13       story to tell.  I didn't even know that we had

        14       female pilots in the Second World War.  And

        15       I'm very proud to know that and to acknowledge

        16       her and to send her this resolution even if

        17       she could not be here.

        18                  Thank you.
